title: Dates and timezones
story:
A timestamp looks like a number. It is closer to a political artefact, and the gap between those two facts is where the bugs live.

Samoa and Tokelau missed an entire day. Friday 30 December 2011 did not happen there — an official change of time zone moved them to the other side of the International Date Line, because being a day behind their trading partners had meant lost business. The government ruled that workers would still be paid for the day that did not exist and that banks could not charge interest across it. No physical quantity changed. A decision was taken, and a date stopped existing in one jurisdiction while continuing to exist everywhere else.

The other end of the scale moves too, and more slowly than the headlines suggest. The 2022 resolution of the General Conference on Weights and Measures is usually reported as abolishing the leap second, and it says nothing of the kind. Resolution 4 decides that the maximum value for the difference between UT1 and UTC will be increased in, or before, 2035 — and then asks the CIPM to consult the ITU and others, propose a new maximum that ensures the continuity of UTC for at least a century, prepare an implementation plan, suggest a review period, and draft a resolution for the meeting in 2026. That is a commitment to raise a tolerance and a request for a proposal, not an abolition. It is also a good illustration of the general rule, which is that the things you are treating as constants are minutes of meetings.

So the practical discipline. Separate the instant from the intent. Something that happened has an instant, and the instant should be stored unambiguously; it is a fact and it will not move. Something that is meant to happen has an intent — nine in the morning, in a named place — and that is not an instant yet, because the rule converting it into one can be changed by a government before the day arrives. Store the local time and the name of the zone, and resolve to an instant at the moment you need one.

Two corollaries worth internalising. A zone is not an offset: an offset is what a zone evaluated to on a particular date, and storing it as though it were the zone throws away the rule and keeps one of its outputs. And the zone rules are data — a database that has to be updated — which means a program that has not been updated is not slightly wrong about the future, it is confidently wrong, using a rule that has been repealed.

problem.name: Instant versus intent
problem.shape: A moment has to be written down, and the rule converting between what a clock reads and what instant it is can be changed by a government after you have written it.
tell: a future appointment is stored as a single absolute instant
a zone is represented by an offset rather than by a name
a scheduled job is defined by a local hour
two systems agree on the number and disagree on the moment
problem.move: Decide whether you are recording something that happened or something that is meant to happen. For the first, store an unambiguous instant. For the second, store the local time and the name of the zone, and resolve to an instant only when you need one. Keep the zone database current, and run schedules on an unambiguous clock, converting for display.
problem.invariant: An instant is a fact and a local time is an intent, and converting between them requires a rule that is in force at a particular date. Only one of the two survives a change to that rule unchanged, and which one depends on what you were recording.
problem.breaks: Storing the intent is right for the future and wrong for the past. A local time plus a zone, applied to a moment that has already occurred, will be re-resolved through whatever rule is current — so a historical event stored that way can move when the rules are amended, which is exactly the failure the approach was adopted to prevent.

cost.time: a conversion at every read rather than one at write, which is arithmetic and cheap
cost.space: two fields where you expected one, plus a zone database that is a dependency rather than a constant
cost.beats: storing an offset, which keeps one evaluation of the rule and discards the rule, and therefore fails in precisely the same way as storing the instant

worked.problem: A meeting is scheduled for nine in the morning, several months from now, in a particular city. What do you store?
worked.reasoning:
Not the instant. Store the local time and the name of the zone, and compute the instant when you need it.

The reason is that a future local time is not yet a point in time. Converting nine in the morning in a particular place into an unambiguous instant requires the offset rule that will be in force on that date, and that rule is set by a government, can change before the date arrives, and has changed with very little notice — Samoa deleted a calendar day by administrative decision. If you resolve the conversion at write time and the rule is amended afterwards, your stored instant is faithful to a rule that no longer exists, and it will resolve back to a wall clock time nobody agreed to. The meeting moves.

If instead you store the local time together with the zone name, you have stored the intent, which is what the participants actually agreed. When the rule changes, the stored data is still correct and the computed instant simply changes with it — which is the behaviour everyone wanted.

The distinction to be explicit about is that a zone is not an offset. An offset is the value a zone evaluated to on some date. Storing the offset keeps one output of the rule and discards the rule, so it fails in exactly the same way as storing the instant.

The converse holds for things that already happened. A logged event has an instant, that instant is a fact, and it should be stored unambiguously — because there is no future rule change that can alter when something occurred. Events get instants; intentions get local time plus a zone.

Two things I would add unprompted. The zone rules are a database that has to be kept current, so a service that has not been updated is not approximately right about the future, it is confidently applying a repealed rule. And any recurring local-time schedule crosses the transitions twice a year, which is why a nightly job at a fixed local hour will one day run twice and one day not at all — a reason to run schedules on an unambiguous clock and convert only for display.
worked.code:
A TIMESTAMP IS NOT A QUANTITY

  Samoa + Tokelau, 2011:
     Friday 30 December DID NOT HAPPEN.
     official time zone change.
     workers still paid for the missing day,
     banks barred from charging interest.

  nothing physical changed.
  a decision was taken.

THE TWO KINDS, AND THEY STORE DIFFERENTLY

  SOMETHING HAPPENED          -> an INSTANT
     a fact. cannot move.
     store it unambiguously.

  SOMETHING IS MEANT TO HAPPEN -> an INTENT
     "09:00, in this named place"
     NOT an instant yet.
     store:  local time + ZONE NAME
     resolve to an instant at USE time.

WHY NOT RESOLVE EARLY

  converting 09:00 -> an instant needs the offset
  rule in force ON THAT DATE.

  that rule is set by a government.
  it can change before the date arrives.

  resolve early, rule changes ->
     your instant is faithful to a repealed rule
     -> it resolves back to a wall clock time
        nobody agreed to.
     THE MEETING MOVES.

A ZONE IS NOT AN OFFSET

  offset = what the zone EVALUATED TO on a date.
  storing the offset keeps one OUTPUT and throws
  away the RULE.
  -> fails identically to storing the instant.

THE HEADLINE, CORRECTED

  "the leap second was abolished in 2022"

  what Resolution 4 actually DECIDES:
     the maximum value for (UT1 - UTC) will be
     increased in, or before, 2035.

  and then REQUESTS a proposal for the new value,
  an implementation plan, a review period, and a
  draft resolution for the 2026 meeting.

  a tolerance raise and a request. not an
  abolition.

problem.practice: Find where your system stores a future time and check whether it stored an instant, an offset, or a zone name. Then take a recurring local-time schedule and work out, on paper, what it does on each of the two transition days — which one runs twice and which one does not run at all.

beats.broke: A timestamp looks like a number and behaves like a political artefact: the rule converting a clock reading into an instant is set by governments and standards bodies, and it changes while your data is sitting still.
beats.fix: Separate the instant from the intent. Store an unambiguous instant for what happened, store local time with the named zone for what is meant to happen, and resolve the second into the first only at the moment of use.
beats.cost: Two fields where you expected one, a zone database that is a live dependency rather than arithmetic, and the acceptance that any future timestamp is a prediction rather than a fact.

interview.q: A meeting is scheduled for nine in the morning, several months from now, in a particular city. What do you store?
interview.trap: Storing it as an instant because that is unambiguous, or storing the offset because that feels like keeping the zone. Both discard the rule and keep one of its outputs, so both silently move the meeting when the rule is amended.
interview.answer:
Not the instant. I would store the local time together with the name of the zone, and compute the instant at the point of use.

A future local time is not yet a point in time. Turning nine in the morning in a named place into an unambiguous instant needs the offset rule that will be in force on that date, and that rule is a political decision — it can be amended before the date arrives, sometimes at short notice. Samoa deleted an entire calendar day by administrative decision, with workers paid for the day that did not exist.

If I resolve the conversion at write time and the rule then changes, the stored instant remains faithful to a rule that no longer exists. It resolves back to a wall clock time nobody agreed to, and the meeting silently moves. Storing local time plus the zone stores what the participants actually agreed, so when the rule changes the data is still correct and the computed instant moves with it — which is the behaviour everyone wanted.

Worth being explicit that a zone is not an offset. An offset is what a zone evaluated to on a particular date, so storing the offset keeps one output of the rule and discards the rule itself, and fails in exactly the same way as storing the instant.

The converse applies to things that already happened: those have instants, the instant is a fact, and no future rule change can alter when something occurred. Events get instants; intentions get local time and a zone.

Two additions. The zone rules are a database that must be kept current, so a service that has not been updated is confidently applying a repealed rule rather than being slightly off. And a recurring local-time schedule crosses the transitions twice a year, which is why a nightly job at a fixed local hour eventually runs twice on one night and not at all on another.

blueprint:
EVENTS GET INSTANTS. INTENTIONS GET ZONES.

   happened      -> instant, stored unambiguously
                    (a fact. no future rule moves it.)

   will happen   -> local time + ZONE NAME
                    resolve at USE time
                    (an intent. the rule may change.)

THE FAILURE, STEP BY STEP

   1. store 09:00 next March as an instant
   2. the government amends the offset rule
   3. your instant is still faithful to the
      OLD rule
   4. it now resolves to 08:00 local
   5. the meeting moved, and nothing errored

A ZONE != AN OFFSET

   offset is what the zone EVALUATED TO,
   on one date.

   keeping the offset = keeping the answer
   and throwing away the question.

THE RULES ARE DATA

   a zone database, updated as governments decide.
   a service that has not updated is not
   approximately right about the future --
   it is confidently applying a REPEALED rule.

TWO WORKED EXAMPLES OF "CONSTANTS" MOVING

   Samoa 2011    a calendar day deleted by
                 administrative decision

   CGPM 2022     "the maximum value for the
                 difference (UT1-UTC) will be
                 increased in, or before, 2035"
                 -- not an abolition. a tolerance
                 raise, and a request for a
                 proposal.

RECURRING LOCAL SCHEDULES

   cross the transitions twice a year
   -> one night the job runs TWICE
   -> one night it does not run at all
   run on an unambiguous clock. convert for
   display only.
takeaway: An instant is a fact and a local time is an intent, and only one of them survives a government changing the rules — which happens, as Samoa showed by deleting 30 December 2011 outright.
